newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico television channels engage in war of words.
newsitem.headline: Mexico television channels engage in war of words.

text.p: Mexico's two biggest television channels engaged in a war of words on Thursday in a dispute that would have been worthy of one of the country's famous soap operas.

Bitter rivals TV Azteca and Televisa traded harsh words after government authorities tried to take legal action against popular TV Azteca talk show hostess Pati Chapoy on allegations of copyright violations.

TV Azteca broadcast images of agents of the Attorney General's Office in front of Chapoy's house as they spent 37 hours trying to detain her, TV Azteca said. Chapoy had a court order that kept her free, the channel added in a statement.
The allegations were that the television star and three others used material from programmes of rival Televisa to make money.
Chapoy vigorously denied the charges as TV Azteca devoted nearly 45 minutes of its main evening news broadcast defending its besieged star.
Televisa, however, fought back. It said that from early 1996, the TV Azteca star was taking Televisa material and selling it.

"The law permits a person to tape a programme for private use, but the law does not allow a person to enter into a theatre and tape the words of an actor, steal the words of an author ... and then sell it without paying for it," Javier Mondragon, a Televisa executive, told a news conference earlier in day.
Mexico's television market is dominated by the powerful Grupo Televisa S.A. and by TV Azteca, privatised from a government channel a few years ago.
TV Azteca has been capturing viewers in Mexico from its larger rival, saying in June that it would have about a third of the country's total television ad market this year.
The upstart channel claimed to have had more viewers than its rival in the capital during the historic July 6 midterm elections in Mexico.
The two channels are also squaring off over broadcasting rights for some of Mexico's most important soccer teams, media analysts said.
Televisa and TV Azteca skirmished last year over allegations tied to financial dealings with Raul Salinas, the jailed brother of former Mexican President Carlos Salinas.
On Thursday a TV Azteca announcer took aim at Televisa, vowing to fight back.
"We are going to compete, but we are going to compete cleanly," the announcer said.
